claims.text: The mechanical and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is controlled by dynamic short-range-order evolution and accompanying local lattice distortions.
Thermal-expansion mismatch during cooling or solidification creates internal stress fields in the alloy.
The internal stress fields produced by SRO-related distortions and thermal-expansion mismatch modulate creep and quasi-static elastic responses.
Controlled aging at 600–800 °C promotes SRO and associated lattice distortions.
Changes in local interatomic potentials caused by SRO generate local lattice distortions.
SRO-related lattice distortions interact with thermal-expansion mismatch to produce internal stresses.
These internal stresses increase resistance to deformation during cold rolling.
These internal stresses modify high-temperature creep behavior.
SRO-related internal stresses change the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli.
Aged, SRO-promoted samples will have higher microhardness after cold rolling than rapidly quenched samples.
Aged, SRO-promoted samples will show delayed creep onset or a reduced tensile-creep rate at 1250 °C relative to rapidly quenched samples.
Aged samples will show shifted elastic-modulus trends over 293–1100 K relative to rapidly quenched samples.
Aged and rapidly quenched samples will exhibit measurable differences in thermal-expansion behavior associated with internal-stress differences.
The rapidly quenched baseline has a more random solid-solution state and minimal SRO.
Diffraction or pair-distribution-function analysis can quantitatively distinguish the SRO levels of the aged and quenched samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if the processing routes produce no statistically significant property differences, or if measured SRO does not correlate with the mechanical and thermoelastic responses.
